units.title: Hello, Smalltalk
units.summary: Print your first lines with Transcript showCr: and learn that in Smalltalk everything is an object that gets messages.

lesson.md: Smalltalk is one of the first object-oriented languages. In Smalltalk, **everything is an object**: numbers, text, even `true` and `false`. You make things happen by sending **messages** to objects. This course uses GNU Smalltalk: you save your code in a file such as `hello.st` and run it with `gst hello.st`. Pharo uses the same language inside a graphical environment.

lesson.code: Transcript showCr: 'Hello, Smalltalk!'.

lesson.md: `Transcript` is an object that shows text. `showCr:` is a message that you send to it: show this text, then start a new line. Text in single quotes, like `'Hello, Smalltalk!'`, is a **string**. The period `.` ends a statement.

lesson.code:
Transcript showCr: 'One'.
Transcript showCr: 'Two'.
Transcript show: 'Three '.
Transcript show: 'and four'.
Transcript cr.

lesson.md: `show:` prints text but stays on the same line. `cr` starts a new line. The statements run from top to bottom, and a period separates each statement from the next one.

Smalltalk can calculate. In `3 + 4`, the object `3` gets the message `+` with the argument `4`, and it answers the object `7`. `showCr:` only accepts strings, so you turn a number into a string with the message `printString`. Parentheses `( )` make Smalltalk calculate the inside first.

lesson.code:
Transcript showCr: (3 + 4) printString.
Transcript showCr: (6 * 7) printString.
Transcript showCr: '3 + 4'.

lesson.md: There is a shorter way to print a single object: send it `displayNl`. It prints the object and starts a new line. `printNl` does the same, but shows the object the way a programmer writes it, so a string keeps its quotes.

lesson.code:
'Hello' displayNl.
'Hello' printNl.
(2 + 3) displayNl.

lesson.md: Every object belongs to a **class**, and you can ask it with the message `class`. A small whole number belongs to `SmallInteger`, text belongs to `String`, and `true` belongs to `True`.

lesson.code:
3 class displayNl.
'Hi' class displayNl.
true class displayNl.

lesson.md: Strings use single quotes. Text in double quotes, like `"note"`, is a **comment**: Smalltalk ignores it. Also do not forget the period between two statements.

card: `show:` stays on the line, `cr` starts a new one
`(3 + 4) printString` turns a number into a string
`x displayNl` prints `x`, `x printNl` prints it as code
`.` ends a statement, `"..."` is a comment

units.title: Messages
units.summary: Send unary, binary and keyword messages, learn the order Smalltalk evaluates them in, and chain messages with cascades.

lesson.md: Everything in Smalltalk happens by sending messages. A message goes to a **receiver**, the object on the left. The name of the message is its **selector**. There are three kinds of messages: unary, binary and keyword messages.

A **unary** message has no argument. It is one word after the receiver. `5 factorial` multiplies 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5, `abs` removes the minus sign, `asUppercase` makes capital letters, and `size` counts the characters of a string.

lesson.code:
5 factorial displayNl.
-7 abs displayNl.
'hello' asUppercase displayNl.
'hello' size displayNl.

lesson.md: A **binary** message has one argument and a name made of symbols, such as `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `<`, `>` and `=`. The comma `,` is a binary message too: it joins two strings.

lesson.code:
(3 + 4) displayNl.
(10 > 3) displayNl.
('Small', 'talk') displayNl.

lesson.md: A **keyword** message has one or more arguments. Each keyword ends with a colon `:` and comes before its argument. `copyFrom: 2 to: 4` is one message with two arguments; its selector is `copyFrom:to:`.

lesson.code:
(3 max: 9) displayNl.
(7 between: 1 and: 10) displayNl.
('hello' copyFrom: 2 to: 4) displayNl.

lesson.md: Smalltalk sends unary messages first, then binary messages, then keyword messages. Binary messages go strictly from left to right, so `2 + 3 * 4` is `20`, not `14`. Use parentheses to choose the order yourself.

lesson.code:
(2 + 3 * 4) displayNl.
(2 + (3 * 4)) displayNl.
(2 + 3 factorial) displayNl.
(3 max: 2 + 5) displayNl.

lesson.md: A semicolon `;` sends another message to the same receiver. This is called a **cascade**. Here all four messages go to `Transcript`.

lesson.code: Transcript show: 'a'; show: 'b'; cr; showCr: 'c'.

lesson.md: In `Transcript showCr: 2 + 3 printString`, the unary message `printString` goes to `3` first, and then `2 + '3'` fails. Write `(2 + 3) printString` instead.

card: Order: unary, then binary (left to right), then keyword
`Transcript show: 'a'; cr` sends both messages to `Transcript`

exercises.explain: Binary messages go before keyword messages, so `2 + 5` is calculated first, and `3 max: 7` is `7`.

units.title: Variables and values
units.summary: Store objects in temporary variables with := and work with integers, fractions, strings, symbols and printString.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for an object. You declare temporary variables between two vertical bars, like `| name age |`. Then you give them a value with `:=`, which you read as "becomes". The declaration comes first, before all statements. Variable names start with a lowercase letter, and longer names look like `totalPrice`.

lesson.code:
| name age |
name := 'Ada'.
age := 36.
Transcript showCr: name.
Transcript showCr: age printString.

lesson.md: A new variable holds `nil`, the object that means "nothing". You can give a variable a new value at any time. In `count := count + 1`, Smalltalk calculates the right side first and then stores the result.

lesson.code:
| count |
count printNl.
count := 5.
count := count + 1.
count printNl.

lesson.md: Whole numbers are **integers**. When `/` cannot divide evenly, Smalltalk keeps the exact result as a **fraction** such as `7/2`. `//` divides and drops the rest, and `\\` gives the remainder. Numbers with a decimal point, like `3.5`, also exist.

lesson.code:
(7 / 2) printNl.
(6 / 3) printNl.
(7 // 2) printNl.
(7 \\ 2) printNl.
((1/3) + (1/6)) printNl.
3.5 printNl.

lesson.md: A string is text in single quotes. The comma `,` joins strings, and `size` counts the characters. To put a single quote inside a string, write it twice: `'It''s'`.

lesson.code:
| greeting |
greeting := 'Hello', ', ', 'world'.
greeting displayNl.
greeting size printNl.
'It''s fine' displayNl.

lesson.md: A **symbol** starts with `#`, like `#red`. Two symbols with the same name are always the very same object. The message `==` checks if two things are the same object.

lesson.code:
#red printNl.
(#red == #red) printNl.
#red size printNl.

lesson.md: `printString` gives the text a programmer writes: strings keep their quotes. `displayString` gives the text for people. `printNl` and `displayNl` print these texts and start a new line.

lesson.code:
'hi' printString displayNl.
'hi' displayString displayNl.
42 printString size printNl.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Compare values, decide with ifTrue:ifFalse: and combine conditions with and:, or: and not.

lesson.md: A comparison like `5 > 3` answers an object: `true` or `false`. These are objects too. `=` checks if two values are equal, `~=` checks if they are different, and `>=` and `<=` mean "at least" and "at most".

lesson.code:
(5 > 3) printNl.
(5 = 3) printNl.
(5 ~= 3) printNl.
(5 >= 5) printNl.
(5 > 3) class printNl.

lesson.md: Smalltalk has no `if` keyword. Instead you send the message `ifTrue:ifFalse:` to a boolean. Its arguments are two pieces of code in square brackets `[ ]`, called **blocks**. Only one of the two blocks runs.

lesson.code:
| age |
age := 20.
age >= 18
    ifTrue: [Transcript showCr: 'adult']
    ifFalse: [Transcript showCr: 'minor'].

lesson.md: You can also send only `ifTrue:` or only `ifFalse:`. When the condition does not match, nothing happens and the program goes on.

lesson.code:
| temp |
temp := 30.
temp > 25 ifTrue: [Transcript showCr: 'hot'].
temp < 10 ifTrue: [Transcript showCr: 'cold'].
Transcript showCr: 'done'.

lesson.md: `ifTrue:ifFalse:` answers the value of the block that ran, so you can store the result. The message `even` answers `true` when a number is even.

lesson.code:
| n label |
n := 7.
label := n even ifTrue: ['even'] ifFalse: ['odd'].
label displayNl.

lesson.md: `and:` answers `true` only when both conditions are true. `or:` answers `true` when at least one is true. The second condition goes into a block, so it only runs when it is needed. `not` turns `true` into `false` and the other way round.

lesson.code:
| x |
x := 15.
((x > 10) and: [x < 20]) printNl.
((x < 0) or: [x > 100]) printNl.
(x > 10) not printNl.

lesson.md: A block can contain another decision. This program checks the first condition, and only when it is false, it checks the second one.

lesson.code:
| score |
score := 75.
score >= 90
    ifTrue: [Transcript showCr: 'A']
    ifFalse: [score >= 70
        ifTrue: [Transcript showCr: 'B']
        ifFalse: [Transcript showCr: 'C']].

lesson.md: Write the code for `ifTrue:` and `ifFalse:` in square brackets `[ ]`, not in parentheses. Also note that `ifFalse` needs its colon: `ifFalse: [ ... ]`.

units.title: Blocks
units.summary: Store code in blocks, run it with value and value:, and give blocks parameters.

lesson.md: A **block** is code in square brackets `[ ]`. The code does not run when Smalltalk reads it. A block is an object, so you can store it in a variable. Send it the message `value` to run it, as often as you like.

lesson.code:
| greet |
greet := [Transcript showCr: 'Hello!'].
Transcript showCr: 'before'.
greet value.
greet value.

lesson.md: When a block runs, it answers the value of its last statement. A block can have several statements, separated by periods.

lesson.code:
| answer |
answer := [3 + 4] value.
answer printNl.
[10. 20. 30] value printNl.

lesson.md: A block can have **parameters**. Each name starts with a colon, and a vertical bar `|` separates the parameters from the code: `[:x | x * 2]`. You run it with `value:` and give the argument.

lesson.code:
| double |
double := [:x | x * 2].
(double value: 5) printNl.
(double value: 21) printNl.

lesson.md: A block with two parameters runs with `value:value:`. The arguments fill the parameters in order. The message `numArgs` tells you how many parameters a block has.

lesson.code:
| add |
add := [:a :b | a + b].
(add value: 3 value: 4) printNl.
add numArgs printNl.

lesson.md: A block can use and change the variables around it. Here the block adds each argument to `total`.

lesson.code:
| total addToTotal |
total := 0.
addToTotal := [:n | total := total + n].
addToTotal value: 5.
addToTotal value: 10.
total printNl.

lesson.md: The number of arguments must match the parameters. Sending `value` to `[:x | x * 2]` is an error, because the block needs one argument.
You already used blocks: `ifTrue: [ ... ]` and `and: [ ... ]` take blocks. The boolean decides if it runs the block or not.

card: `[ ... ]` is a block, `aBlock value` runs it
A block answers its last statement

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with timesRepeat:, count with to:do:, loop with whileTrue: and visit every element with do:.

lesson.md: In Smalltalk, loops are messages that take blocks. `timesRepeat:` runs its block a given number of times.

lesson.code: 3 timesRepeat: [Transcript showCr: 'Hello'].

lesson.md: `1 to: 4 do: [:i | ... ]` counts from `1` to `4`. Each round, the block gets the current number as its argument. A loop often updates a variable, like `sum` here.

lesson.code:
| sum |
sum := 0.
1 to: 4 do: [:i |
    Transcript showCr: i printString.
    sum := sum + i].
Transcript showCr: 'sum: ', sum printString.

lesson.md: `to:by:do:` counts in steps. With a negative step, it counts down.

lesson.code: 10 to: 1 by: -3 do: [:i | Transcript showCr: i printString].

lesson.text: Repeat while a condition is true

lesson.md: `whileTrue:` repeats its block as long as a condition is true. The condition is a block too, because Smalltalk must check it again before every round. `whileFalse:` repeats as long as the condition is false.

lesson.code:
| n |
n := 1.
[n < 50] whileTrue: [n := n * 3].
n printNl.

lesson.md: `do:` runs a block once for every element of a collection. `#(3 5 7)` is an **array** literal: a list of values after `#`, in parentheses. A string is a collection too: its elements are characters, written like `$a`.

lesson.code:
#(3 5 7) do: [:x | (x * x) printNl].
'abc' do: [:ch | ch printNl].

lesson.md: If the condition of `whileTrue:` never becomes false, the loop never ends. Make sure the block changes something that the condition checks.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
| n |
n := 0.
4 timesRepeat: [n := n + 5].
n printNl.
exercises.explain: The block runs four times and adds `5` each time.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?

1 to: 10 by: 4 do: [:i | s := s + i].
s printNl.
exercises.explain: The loop visits `1`, `5` and `9`. The next step would be `13`, which is past `10`. `1 + 5 + 9` is `15`.

exercises.explain: `n` becomes `2`, `4`, `8`, `16` and `32`. Then `32 < 20` is false and the loop stops.

exercises.explain: `to:do:` counts up. From `5` up to `1` there is no number, so it prints nothing. Use `to:by:do:` with `-1`.

units.title: Collections
units.summary: Store many objects in an Array or OrderedCollection and work with them using do:, collect:, select: and inject:into:.

lesson.md: A **collection** holds many objects. An **Array** has a fixed size. You write an array literal as `#(2 3 5)`. The first element has the index `1`. `at:` reads an element, and `first`, `last` and `size` do what their names say.

lesson.code:
| primes |
primes := #(2 3 5 7 11).
primes size printNl.
(primes at: 1) printNl.
primes last printNl.
primes printNl.

lesson.md: `Array new: 3` makes an array with three empty places, which all hold `nil`. `at:put:` stores an object at an index. The cascade sends all three `at:put:` messages to the same array.

lesson.code:
| colors |
colors := Array new: 3.
colors at: 1 put: 'red'; at: 2 put: 'green'; at: 3 put: 'blue'.
(colors at: 2) displayNl.
colors printNl.

lesson.md: An **OrderedCollection** can grow. `add:` puts an element at the end, `addFirst:` at the front, and `removeFirst` takes the first element out and answers it. `includes:` checks if an element is there.

lesson.code:
| list |
list := OrderedCollection new.
list add: 'tea'; add: 'milk'; addFirst: 'bread'.
list printNl.
list size printNl.
(list includes: 'milk') printNl.
list removeFirst displayNl.
list printNl.

lesson.md: `collect:` answers a new collection with the result of the block for each element. `select:` keeps the elements for which the block answers `true`, and `reject:` keeps the others. `detect:` answers the first element that matches.

lesson.code:
| nums |
nums := #(1 2 3 4 5 6).
(nums collect: [:n | n * n]) printNl.
(nums select: [:n | n even]) printNl.
(nums reject: [:n | n even]) printNl.
(nums detect: [:n | n > 3]) printNl.

lesson.md: `inject:into:` combines all elements into one value. It starts with the first argument. For each element, the block gets the result so far and the element, and its answer becomes the new result.

lesson.code:
| nums |
nums := #(1 2 3 4).
(nums inject: 0 into: [:sum :n | sum + n]) printNl.
(nums inject: 1 into: [:product :n | product * n]) printNl.

lesson.md: These messages work on every collection, also on strings. `isVowel` answers `true` for the characters `a`, `e`, `i`, `o` and `u`, so `'hello' select: [:c | c isVowel]` answers `'eo'`.
Indexes start at `1`, not at `0`. `#(10 20) at: 0` and `#(10 20) at: 3` are errors.

card: `#(1 2 3)` is an Array, `at: 1` is the first element

units.title: Classes
units.summary: Define your own classes with instance variables and methods, return values with ^ and create objects with new.

lesson.md: Every object is an instance of a class. A class describes what its instances store, the **instance variables**, and which messages they understand, the **methods**. In GNU Smalltalk, you define a class with `Object subclass: Counter [ ... ]`. `new` creates an instance.

lesson.code:
Object subclass: Counter [
    | count |
    reset [ count := 0 ]
    increment [ count := count + 1 ]
    count [ ^count ]
]

| c |
c := Counter new.
c reset.
c increment.
c increment.
c count printNl.

lesson.md: `| count |` declares an instance variable: every counter has its own `count`. `reset [ ... ]` defines a method with the name `reset`, and the code in its brackets runs when the object gets the message `reset`. The caret `^` returns a value from a method. A method and an instance variable may have the same name, like `count` here.
A method with an argument has a keyword name and a parameter name, like `deposit: amount [ ... ]`. Inside a method, `self` is the object itself, so `self balance` sends `balance` to the same object.

lesson.code:
Object subclass: Account [
    | balance |
    Account class >> new [ ^super new init ]
    init [ balance := 0 ]
    balance [ ^balance ]
    deposit: amount [ balance := balance + amount ]
    canPay: amount [ ^amount <= self balance ]
]

| acc |
acc := Account new.
acc deposit: 50; deposit: 25.
acc balance printNl.
(acc canPay: 100) printNl.

lesson.md: `Account class >> new [ ... ]` is a **class method**: the class itself understands it. `super new` creates the object in the normal way, and then `init` gives `balance` its start value `0`. Without `init`, `balance` would be `nil`.

A **subclass** gets all instance variables and methods of its superclass. It can add methods or replace them. Here `Dog` replaces `speak`, and `describe` uses the new version. An object without its own way to print shows its class name, like `a Dog`.

lesson.code:
Object subclass: Animal [
    | name |
    Animal class >> named: aName [ ^self new setName: aName ]
    setName: aName [ name := aName ]
    speak [ ^'...' ]
    describe [ ^name, ' says ', self speak ]
]

Animal subclass: Dog [
    speak [ ^'Woof' ]
]

(Dog named: 'Rex') describe displayNl.
(Animal named: 'Tom') describe displayNl.
(Dog named: 'Rex') printNl.
lesson.output:
Rex says Woof
Tom says ...
a Dog

lesson.md: Pharo uses the same classes and methods. Instead of a file, you type each class and method into the system browser of the graphical environment.
A method without `^` answers the object itself, not the value of its last line. If you write `count [ count ]`, then `c count` answers `a Counter`.

card: `Object subclass: Point [ | x y | ... ]` defines a class
`setX: n [ x := n ]` is a method with an argument
`Point class >> new [ ^super new init ]` is a class method

exercises.prompt: What does `^` do in a method?
options: It returns a value from the method
It raises a number to a power
exercises.explain: `^` ends the method and answers the value after it.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
Object subclass: Box [
    | width |
    width: n [ width := n ]
    doubled [ ^width * 2 ]
]

| b |
b := Box new.
b width: 21.
b doubled printNl.
exercises.explain: `width:` stores `21` in the instance variable, and `doubled` returns `21 * 2`.

]

Greeter new greet printNl.
exercises.explain: The method has no `^`, so it answers the object itself, which prints as `a Greeter`.

exercises.statement: Every instance of a class has its own copy of the instance variables.
exercises.explain: Two counters can have different values for `count`. Each object stores its own instance variables.

Circle new describe displayNl.
exercises.explain: `self name` goes to the circle, and `Circle` replaces `name` with its own method.

exercises.explain: In Smalltalk, `^` returns a value. There is no `return` keyword.

p name: 'Ada'.
